utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have today's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's Matthew Olmsted and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence this morning, appearing Igor Pantelic and Miroslav Cuskic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Olmsted, I gather that there are some matters that we need to -- to which we need to turn our minds before the witness -- first witness comes in?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, sorry. The first is an oral application to add some documents to the 65 ter exhibit list. As Your Honours are probably now informed, we received some documents just yesterday that is -- that are relevant to the next witness. We interviewed the next witness approximately a year ago, and he turned over a number of documents in his personal collection at that time that were relevant to this case, and we produced those to the Defence and we will be showing a number of those to the witness today. It was a two-day interview and after the first day we said, Go home, if you find any other documents please turn those over to us as well. The second interview went and he did not produce any additional documents. However, yesterday afternoon during proofing he turned over seven pages of documents that we've deemed as relevant to our case and that we would like on our 65 ter exhibit list. I believe this is a scenario that we've discussed before where a witness produces documents during a proofing session. This is probably a quintessential situation where the party calling that witness has good cause to seek to amend their 65 ter exhibit list so long as they can show that the documents are relevant and that there is undo prejudice to the other side. I don't know if Your Honours have had a chance to look at the documents, but our position is they are relevant because -- well, they are relevant to our JCE charges as they show co-ordination and co-operation between various components witness the municipality, the Territorial Defence, the police, the Crisis Staffs, the militaries. This is, of course, the best witness to testify about them because he produced them, he can authentic them, also given his position back in 1992 he is a good witness to talk about them. With regard to prejudice, we don't believe that the Defence will be prejudice by adding these documents to the 65 ter exhibit at this time. The documents more or less corroborates the -- or the evidence that this witness provided during his interview. We don't think they go beyond the scope of his interview, and therefore they really don't constitute any surprise for the Defence. I've spoken to the Defence and they -- so if I understand it, their position is they, of course, object in principle to addition of documents at this stage but since the remedy typically in these in instances is additional time, as I understand it, they would be okay if they could begin their cross-examination, at least as to these documents, on Friday. We do not have another witness this week other than this witness and this is due to the fact that the last two witnesses went a lot faster than predicted, and the next witness after this one is under subpoena so we can't bring him forward, and we've definitely scrambled to try to find another witness to come this week but we have just been unable to do it on such a short time-frame. And so I think we do have the time, if necessary, to give the Defence additional opportunity to review the documents and to cross-examine this witness on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have the documents been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, they have all been translated. Last afternoon we produced translation -- a partial translation, and then I sent an e-mail out I think around 6.30, 7.00 p.m. for the remaining documents, so they've all been translated and I believe the Case Manager will have them loaded in e-court within the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I hear from Defence counsel, when do you anticipate -- you -- you mentioned that they've raised the possibility of deferring their cross-examination until Friday. When did you anticipate completing your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we've asked for four hours with this witness. There is a number of documents, and we're going to definitely seek to complete it within that time. There are a lot of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, could we hear from the Defence on this application?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't have a LiveNote. None of the computer is on our side. I don't know what is the situation ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It is in the process of being corrected, I am given to understand, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, we do object, of course, on such a short notice that ten documents be introduced. But we understand the situation as Mr. Olmsted explained to us. Now, we believe the guide-lines say that it has be a written motion. That is number one. The second thing is Mr. Olmsted is now offering some translations. Is it -- is it an official translation or is it a draft translation by the OTP? Because I believe we -- we discussed this sometime ago, that only the CLSS translation should be accepted as -- as a translation that can be admitted into the -- into the case as an exhibit. That's the second thing. And the third thing, yes, we -- we discussed this with the witness -- Mr. Olmsted, and if we would be given some additional time for preparation for our cross we would be able to -- to start our cross on -- on Friday. I mean, based on these -- these documents. That was the gist of -- of our conversation that we had with Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I call on Mr. Pantelic, please tell me if I summarise your position correctly. Your objection is as a matter of principle; but, substantively, having regard to the practical circumstances in which these documents came to the knowledge of the Prosecution, you raise no substantive objection, save that you be given adequate time to able to deal with, which, as present estimates indicate, you should be in a position to do by Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness is not related to our client, so we actually -- as a matter of principle just support Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Having regard to the position taken by the Defence and bearing in mind that the guide-lines are guide-lines and not a straight jacket. In other words, they are intended to facilitate and not frustrate the progress of a trial, in the circumstances, having regard, especially to the recency of the knowledge of the Prosecution in this regard, we accede to the application that they be added to the 65 ter -- -- the Prosecution may add these documents to the 65 ter list. And the -- Mr. Zecevic, is it necessary for us to rule now on your application for an adjournment or can that be deferred until you begin your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I'm -- whatever pleases the Court. We are fine, even it is deferred before we start our cross-examination. But, Your Honours, there is one thing, we need the LiveNote once the witness comes in, because that is what we are -- we are marking it for, for the purposes of cross-examination. And we still don't have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Did I understand there was another preliminary matter that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And we'd have to go into private session to discuss that. It's with regard to protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. We are considering a brief adjournment so that the technical correction could be made to bring up the LiveNote. Could we deal with this new matter or should this also wait until we have LiveNote? I think we can proceed, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think we can, because what the Defence is saying is they need the LiveNote during his substantive testimony. This is dealing with a preliminary matter I doubt they're going to cross-examine him on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have been alerted, though, I suspect that before we rule on this matter, we may have to hear from the witness. Because it's a new application.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we informed the witness of that fact. And he's coming ready to present his situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry that was the second matter that I wanted to raise prior to this witness's testimony was that there was a protective measures matter for this witness, that we should go to private session to discuss it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you were interviewed by the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor in March of last year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's correct that we had an interview in March last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to that interview, were you advised of your rights to have counsel present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The complete procedure has been made clear to me before the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, you agreed to be interviewed without counsel back -- last year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of that interview, were you satisfied with how the interview was conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was satisfied. Everything was fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about your professional background with the police. Did you begin working for the MUP or, at the time it was known as the SUP, in Bosnia in November of 1986?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. In November 1986, I started working in what was then the Secretariat of Internal Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the first position you held with the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first job was fire inspector, republican fire inspector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, before we venture too far into the curriculum vitae of this witness, I wonder if you want to go into private session for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we should, Your Honours. That's a very good suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Should I continue for the next few minutes, or should we take our break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you make practical use of the next three minutes [Microphone not activated] or -- yes, are you about to begin a line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was asking whether you could make practical use of the next three minutes, or are you about to embark on a line of questions which you prefer not to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me give it a shot, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the conflict in Vlasenica, was Vlasenica municipality a multi-ethnic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately what percentage of the population in the municipality was Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, but it was perhaps in a 50/50 ratio. In the urban centre of Vlasenica, it could have been up to 58 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "58 per cent," 58 per cent Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other 50 per cent, would that be Croat or Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly Serb. Because, traditionally, in that area, there were few Croats. Not even 1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the multi-party elections in 1990, were these percentages that you just described for us reflected in the police force at the SJB Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Like in all other agencies, that ratio was respected, following the principle of equal ethnic representation, proportional ethnic representation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened after the multi-party elections with regard to the ethnic mix of the police force in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, that principle of ethnic representation remained the same and the ratio remained the same until the 21st of April, which was the beginning, and we'll talk about that later. But something else changed. The leading positions in various services from the station commander to the chief of the CID were no longer appointed by the professional hierarchy but by political parties. So a Serb was appointed chief; a Bosniak was appointed commander; chief of the CID also Bosniak. But that was according to the compromise and agreement among the political parties, and even the minister probably couldn't influence that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just clarify one thing you said. I think you referred to the appointment of the CID. Would that be the SJB chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The centre of public security, CJB that is correct's the acronym.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to clarify, these political appointments to these positions within the police force, that they included the SJB chief as well as the commanders at the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a proposal from the political leadership, so through the minister and the chief of the centre, these proposals were sent and their approval was probably sought. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's a good time for us to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I resume?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after the multi-party elections in 1990, who became the chief of SJB Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, the public security station in Vlasenica was headed by Radomir Bjelanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did he replace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Midhad Huremovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of Midhad Huremovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who proposed Bjelanovic for the position of chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said that, in the negotiations among the parties, he was put forth by the SDS, and this proposal was then forwarded to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Bjelanovic's experience in law enforcement, prior to his appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not work in the Ministry of the Interior anywhere. He worked in the bauxite company. He was the director of the work community, or something like that. He was a mining engineer. He worked in various positions in the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to 1992, how would you describe the relations between the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let us go back to the period from 1985 to the multi-party elections. We can say that their relations were good. It functioned well in Vlasenica, because, at that time, it was one of the better developed, better organised municipalities. After the multi-party elections, the situation got polarised, just as it did everywhere else, and the relations deteriorated day by day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the creation of the Serb Autonomous Regions in BiH in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, officially, not. But through various rumours and through the media which did not cover that extensively, but I was able to garner some knowledge but no specifics, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who created these SAOs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the idea was launched by the SDS leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you know, what was the purpose of these Serb Autonomous Regions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the purpose was to establish some kind of autonomy over a certain area as its very name indicated. And if we were to analyse this topic, although I haven't really prepared for that, those in Serb Autonomous Regions encompassed areas with a Serb majority. But there were other ethnic communities present. But the areas were those where Serbs were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if Vlasenica was a part of a Serb Autonomous Region, back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, an autonomous region, Birac, of Birac, was established at that time. But I did not notice any impact of its creation. But it did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who among the political leadership from Vlasenica was associated with this Serb Autonomous Region of Birac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, given that I had worked in the Ministry of the Interior for a long time, I can tell you that by 1989 it was already prohibited that -- for us to be politically active. We were supposed to be professional, a professional service. But as a citizen, as a private citizen, I learned that Milenko Stanic, who was the president of the municipality at the time, was involved in those activities. So for as long as this SAO Birac continued to function, he was the president of the government of that Autonomous Region of Birac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this SAO Birac was formed, what did the SDS form in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the SAO Birac was formed, I don't know the date when it happened. But no impact was felt of its creation. Some strategic decisions were made at the level of the party, but, on the ground, in the institutions, everything continued to function just as it had before, with the application of the representation system that I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 3103.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document is entitled: "Decision to found Assembly of the Serbian people in the Municipality of Vlasenica." And it's dated 24 October 1991. Sir, do you recall that this was one of the documents that you provided to us, to the Prosecutor, during your interview last year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 2 of both of the B/C/S and the English. And if we look under Roman numeral VIII, it states that: "The Serbian Vlasenica municipality shall remain part of the autonomous region of Birac and shall also be the capital of the region." Sir, do you know why Vlasenica was chosen as the capital of the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell you why, but -- because of it -- its geography, well, that's -- its location, and as I already mentioned, Milenko Stanic, the president of the municipality who became the president of the government of the SAO Birac, well, the seat was there, so that was probably one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I tender this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1055, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point, did the SDS create a Serb Crisis Staff in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me, I was not active in the party. These documents are the documents that I found and studied, and I consider them to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since you brought them up, where did you find these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found some of those documents in the files kept by my predecessor, Radomir Bjelanovic. I simply found them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And obtained them in this manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find them at the SJB Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2897.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now this document is entitled: "Decision on the Establishment of a Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Vlasenica and its Responsibilities." Is this another document that you provided us, that you found at SJB Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of this decision, it says: "The decision was made following instructions from the Main Board of BiH SDS regarding operations under conditions of imminent threat of war." Sir, do you know what those SDS Main Board instructions were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. I have never seen them, but I learnt about them from these documents, because they are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under Roman numeral II, it lists ten members of the Crisis Staff. Can you tell us what are the ethnicities of these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've already discussed Milenko Stanic. Who was Bozo Milic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bozo Milic was a member of the party; and later on, he was appointed the president of the Executive Board of the Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 9, it lists commander of the TO, which I understand is the Territorial Defence, as a member of this Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under the old rules that governed the Territorial Defence, it was Bosko Nastic. And after the Crisis Staff was established, that post was taken by Bozidar Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Stanimirovic was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 10, it lists the chief of the public security station as a member of the Crisis Staff. At the time of this decision, who would have that been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radomir Bjelanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what authority did the SDS Crisis Staff have over SJB Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff, as is indicated here, assumed the functions of the Municipal Assembly and the explanation given was that given the circumstances the Municipal Assembly could no longer function, and this is why the Crisis Staff was established. In that period, the Crisis Staff at least tried to influence the operation of the Ministry of the Interior, or, rather, of the public security station. In many situations, we who knew what the ministry actually is and what the chain of command should look like, and the minister himself insisted on that. We tried to oppose in each and every one of those situations. We always wanted to keep the MUP as a professional institution, as a professional service, but in some cases, the influence was so strong that we couldn't resist the pressure that was exerted on us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever an occasion in 1992 when the SJB chief in Vlasenica, and that includes yourself once you assumed that role, was subordinated to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not formally. But they tried in every way they could to influence the decision-making and the functioning, the organisation, the personnel matters and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Crisis Staff would attempt to influence your work as SJB [realtime transcript read in error "Secretary-General"] chief or your predecessor as SJB chief, would you report this problem up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did that once I formally became the chief, so from August on. I would always provide reports to my immediate superior, either in writing or orally; that was the centre chief Zoran Cvijetic. And I'm sure that he, in turn, reported all that to the minister. There were situations where we would receive feedback as to how -- what position to take on certain matters and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just -- I have been alerted to a correction on the record on line 25 of page 26, it says: "Was there ever an occasion in 1992 when the Secretary-General chief in Vlasenica, and that includes you." It's actually the SJB chief. Were you aware whether Bjelanovic attended the Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't confirm that with certainty, but I assume that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else from SJB Vlasenica would attend these Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, it was the chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about yourself? Once you assumed the role of SJB chief, did you attend at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time, the Crisis Staff no longer existed. It was the War Commission, or the War Presidency that existed at the time. The situation was different. I think that by mid-June the Crisis Staff was disbanded, possibly by an order from higher up, and the War Commissions were established. So, at the time when I could act on behalf of the station, it no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, we have been through this issue before. But I would like to hear the witness's opinion about why the Crisis Staffs were demolished or abolished and replaced by the War Commissions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I probably can't give you a relevant answer, but I can give you my opinion. Since things were developing very quickly, the war broke out and so on, the leadership at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as it was at the time, decided as a strategic decision to disband the Crisis Staffs in order to create a chain of command that would enable it control the whole area and to eliminate the arbitrary decisions or willfulness on the part of the Crisis Staffs in various municipalities, because they strove to become as independent as they could of the legal structure that was in the offing, that was being built in Republika Srpska. That's how I see it. And, well, I did have a document somewhere but sometime in June the President of the republic decided that municipal commissions be established in order to create this system of subordination. So that's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You -- you are probably correct in your assumption. But could you explain to us just how the strings of command and control were strengthened in the War Commissions, compared to the previous situations when the Crisis Staffs were having power? Just how did the War Commissions become stronger and more disciplined under the MUP's control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just one detail in all that. The Presidency of the Serbian Republic appointed people to each municipality, or region. People whose task it was was to establish the commissions set to replace the Crisis Staffs, and they reported directly to the Presidency of the republic. To be more specific, in the region where we were, in Birac, there was this man Djokanovic. He was the commissioner. There was another man in charge of another region and so on, but I know about Djokanovic. I don't know his first name. So he headed the commission. And the other members were from the local structures, from the municipality. And that's how they functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we tender this document in front of us into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1056, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did there come a time when you stopped travelling to Tuzla for your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- when -- when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, sometime in April or March, some groups, paragroups, were established, check-points were set up. And then, on the 21st of April, in Vlasenica, when the conflict broke out, I stopped travelling to Tuzla, because I had to go there on Monday and on Friday, and, if needed, even more often. I had to go to the headquarters of our service where we would agree what to do, in terms of fire protection. But for as long as telephone lines were up, I was able to keep in contact with Nedim Kurbasic, my boss at the time. I would call him from time to time and he told me it's dangerous to travel. If there's no need for you to travel, don't go, we'll keep in touch by phone. It functioned like that until early May when the telephone lines were disrupted. After that, could I no longer communicate with him. But given the circumstances and the nature of our job, which was fire protection and explosive protection, there was no need for us to do that job anymore, so I no longer travelled after the end of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point did the Serb Crisis Staff take over power in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we begin discussing the takeover itself, I would like to discuss the three weeks in April leading up to the takeover. First, during this pre-takeover period, were there any changes in the composition of the police force at Vlasenica SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean before the 21st of April?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the ethnic composition, no. There were no changes. The only difference was the admission of an increased number of reserve police officers, who were admitted in accordance with the representation system that was in place. Serbs, Bosniaks, there were very few Croats there. So maybe one or two Croats. But, I, as a person who had an office there merely and actually did something else, I could discern that the relationship had changed and that groups were being established. There was a group of people who was close to the commander, Fadil Hadzic, and there was another group that was closer to the station chief, Bjelanovic, who was a Serb. So you could see how situation was becoming polarised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what the security situation was like in Vlasenica during this pre-conflict time-period, the three weeks leading up to the 21 April takeover.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The takeover was long expected. Nobody knew when it would take place, but people were talking about it, because it was obvious that something was in the offing there. But in terms of security, the situation was not bad. There were no security risks, but you could feel it in the air that something was brewing. We, as the Ministry of Interior - we, the police, if I could call us that - we who tried to do our job as professionals in the name of the people, it was actually the most difficult for us to find out what would happen, because nobody trusted us because the SDA people and the SDS people did not trust us. So we did get some information, but we tried to create an atmosphere, a climate, we set up joint patrols, I took part there them. We would patrol the town at night in order to reassure the people as much as we could. We would patrol by car through all the neighbourhoods and streets, but there was nobody around. People hunkered down in their homes. They were just sitting there and waiting for something to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'll just remind you to try to keep your answers short, and I can always ask you some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So prior to the conflict, prior to 21 April, if I understand you correctly there was no armed resistance by either the Muslims or the Serbs in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you hear during this time-period -- or, actually, any time prior to the conflicts, about the arming of Serbs, local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This arming did occur, both among Serbs and Bosniaks. But they were rather discreet about it, and it was difficult for us to get any information. And even our joint patrols failed to catch them at it. But we knew it was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the information that you did have, who was actually arming the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapons were mainly from the former JNA. That was the source of arming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your interview, you mentioned the SDS was participating in the arming. Was that the case or -- or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely. The SDS, in concord with the JNA, supplied quantities of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this pre-21 April time-period, were you aware that the RS MUP had been established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I and the public security station did not operate according to this new scheme, but we knew that the new MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2898.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a Crisis Staff decision, entitled: "Decision on an Imminent Threat of war," from 19 April 1992. Is this another document that you provided during your last interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to this decision, an imminent threat of war was declared and if -- the first reason was: "... as a result of disrupted interethnic relations." Can you tell us what that was referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you can see the primary motivation for this decision. Seven or ten days before the 21st of April, all the leading representatives of the Bosniak people headed by the then-President of the SDA, left Vlasenica. That was on the one hand. On the other hand, they availed themselves of this opportunity to proclaim this imminent threat of war because the Assembly was no longer able to operate without a significant number of MPs, and that's why this decision was taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It provides as another reason that there were outside threats. What outside threat was the municipality facing on 19 April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know specifically what you mean, but in our broader region, Vlasenica is bordered by Kladanj, Zvenice [phoen], Zepa, Srebrenica, and information came through that units were being organised there as well. I don't know what else it could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also gives as a reason for this decision, mass migration of the population from the municipality. Members of which ethnic group were leaving en masse from the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period, let's say from the 4th of April until the 21st April when this happened, both Bosniaks and Serbs left the municipality en masse. Bosniaks were going towards Tuzla, Sarajevo, Kladanj; whereas, Serbs mainly took their families away left them somewhere there Serbia. That -- that's the kind of migration that was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were they leaving the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been the uncertainty and the potential danger to families. Because based on the existing experience and estimates from Slovenia and Croatia, it was felt that something could happen to us as well, and families were placed somewhere where it was safer, in Serbia for Serbs, or in Tuzla and Sarajevo for Bosniaks. That made people feel safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, before we leave this document, I'd just like to elicit from the witness some information on the background for this, because the document leaves the impression that the declaration of an imminent threat of war was left to some very local institutions. And so my question is: Was there a similar declaration of an imminent threat of war coming from above, from the government, that would enable each of the local authorities to declare, on their own, whether or not they thought that there was now an imminent threat of war in their little region.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose, because I was not one of the main players. But I suppose it was done in coordination with the highest leadership of the SDS, for instance, or at their suggestion, or based on their evaluations. That's how these decisions must have been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that question. At the ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the top of the document it says that this discussion was made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I just need to give the floor to the registrar to assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So 65 ter 2898 becomes Exhibit P1057, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just -- if we can keep this document up on the screen, it says in the first paragraph of the document that this decision was made pursuant to a decision of the National Security Council of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did you know what this National Security Council was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that these organs existed but I was not particularly knowledgeable about their competencies and activities. Because we're still talking about a period up to the 21st of April, wherein my immediate environment at the station nothing much changed within the organisation and the municipality still functioned the same way. The president of the Executive Board, the Bosniak, was still there. So all these structures operated as before, although something was simmering already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, for interruption. But I believe we have a problem with the translation of this document. The translation which is provided is not accurate, because the original says: Based on the decision of the Assembly, then, comma, the national -- the National Security Council, then, again, comma, the Crisis Staff takes -- of Vlasenica takes this decision. Which, according to me, means that there is, first, the decision of the Assembly, and then, after that, the decision of the Nationality Security Council. And, therefore, the -- the translation is not -- is not correct. Because it doesn't -- it says National Security Council of the Assembly, such a body didn't exist in Republika Srpska at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zecevic, what am I to make of this? Was the decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- taken in Vlasenica taken in accordance with a decision taken from a higher level?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not -- I'm not -- I don't want to -- to mix into the testimony of the witness. Witness will tell us if he knows or doesn't know. I'm just referring to the translation of the document. It appears to me from this document that is there a decision of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. Then, after that, the executive body of the Assembly which is the National Security Council, and -- and the Crisis Staff. Because that is what they referred to in the -- in the preamble of this document. If it's right or wrong, I cannot confirm at this point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. I just wasn't sure about which assembly you were referring to. But now I understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So should the witness be referred to the original in B/C/S and asked to read into the record what it says and see what the interpreters make of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That sounds reasonable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you read the first paragraph of this document that's in front of you, for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Pursuant to a decision of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Nationality Security Council, the Crisis Staff of the Vlasenica municipality, at its session held on 19 April 1992, adopts the following decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. It -- it doesn't -- the witness didn't say "its National Security Council." Oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. It has been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I proceed? We've addressed this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I stand corrected, but what we have here, it's page 38, line 4 -- actually, 5, it says the "nationality Security Council d of the municipality Crisis Staff." I'm lost. I'm lost. So my suggestion would be to ask from our learned friends from the interpretation unit to clarify preamble of B/C/S and English version. I don't want to suggest, but, I mean, I -- I -- I'm fully supporting Mr. Zecevic submission. It's very simple. In English version it should be: "Pursuant to a decision of the Assembly of Serbian republic Bosnia and Herzegovina, national security" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, rather than your volunteering to assist in the translation and interpretation of this, the -- the prudent course would be to invoke the established procedure for correcting this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at another document, 65 ter 2900. Now what we have before us is another Crisis Staff decision entitled: "Decision to Take Over Power in the Area of the Municipality of Vlasenica," and also from 19 April 1992. Sir, was this another document you provided during your last interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under Roman numeral II of this decision, it provides that the reason for establishing a Serbian Assembly was that the Joint Assembly could not have functioned because the assemblymen and officials of Muslim ethnicity are leaving. I think you touched on this previously. But what was the Joint Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this document, we see the reason why they decided to take this decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. My question to you is: This Joint Assembly, could you explain to us what that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Joint Assembly was an assembly where, according to the electoral results from 1991, MPs were represented, both Serbs and Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we look at -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1058, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. May we look at 65 ter 2902.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is another Crisis Staff decision entitled: "Decision to Disarm Citizens Possessing Fire-arms Illegally," also dated 19 April 1992. Sir, to whom was this decision directed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This decision was directed at the competent authorities, the Ministry of Interior, the TO Staff; and it also refers to JNA units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's calling for citizens to turn in their fire-arms by a set date. Would that be citizens of one particular ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision says it applies to all the citizens who own weapons illegally. And when this decision was enforced, that's how it started. Everyone started surrendering weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Serbs also possessed illegal weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the outset, yes, they did. They did own weapons. And, at the beginning, both Serbs and Bosniaks started turning in weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you may have answered my next question. What was the Muslim population's reaction to this decision? Did they comply with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some understood it literally, that they should return even weapons for which they had a licence, and they started bringing in hunting rifles and pistols they had licences for. But those who had automatic weapons, Kalashnikovs and such, did not turn in weapons, and they did not want to be exposed, because they obtained them illegally in the first place and kept them in hiding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was this decision communicated to the population of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, since I was also called to come to the police station that morning at 9.00 to turn in my weapon, since we, the members of the MUP, were issued with automatic rifles in September 1991 and we also had our service pistols, I was called on the 21st to come to the station and bring my weapons. There was some men there masked and told me that we should turn our weapons. And I said, Here is my weapon but please give me a receipt because this is a service gun. I'm a member of the MUP, and this is government issue. And they said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to that, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is with regard to this document which is directed, it appears, to the citizens of Vlasenica, and how that decision was communicated to the general population and not the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I believe the -- the witness's answer wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you answer that question, if you go back to your prior response, I think the last bit, you say, "I'm a member of the MUP and this is government issue. And they said ..." and from there on, the interpreter was unable to catch what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I was a member of the MUP and sometime around 9.00 in the morning I was called from the police station to bring my weapon, or weapons. Since I had a service pistol as a member of the ministry, and back in September 1991, we members of the MUP, or at least some of us, were also issued an automatic weapon, a Kalashnikov, I obeyed and brought my weapons to the police station. I was met by some masked young men who had their faces masked and wore camouflage uniforms. And I said, I brought my weapons, give me a receipt, because this is service weaponry of the ministry that I was issued with. But the answer was, Leave this here and disappear upstairs, and I really did go to an office upstairs and spent some time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's return to my question which is how the decision in front of you, which is aimed at the citizenry of Vlasenica, how was this decision conveyed to the population? By what mens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Already, early in the morning I was still at home. You could hear something being announced in the streets of the town through a public address system mounted on an APC and on a Volkswagen Golf. The announcement was that weapons should be turned in. They were obviously reading from a script that citizens should return, or turn in weapons to the closest military JNA unit or to the police station, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Golf Volkswagen, to what organ did that vehicle belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was the only Golf Mark II. It was a blue and white car that belonged to the public security station in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1059, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could have on the screen, 65 ter 2899.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is another Crisis Staff decision, entitled: "Decision to Disarm the Active and Reserve Forces of the Vlasenica Public Security Station," from 19 April 1992. Sir, was this decision, which I think you were referring to a moment ago, was this decision lawful? Could the Serb Crisis Staff order the police to disarm themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. There was the former MUP of the BiH which ceased to exist -- to function, and then the Serbian MUP was formed. And I think that, in accordance with the hierarchy in the MUP, no minister, no assistant would ever sign this decision. They would seek some correction. They would seek an explanation as to who needs to be disarmed in actual fact, and they would not sign it the way it stands here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago you mentioned that the Crisis Staff would occasionally attempt to influence the police in Vlasenica. Would this be an example of that type of attempt at influencing the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A classic example where my predecessor, Mr. Bjelanovic, must have been taken aback. And I assume that he reported to the minister and sought instructions as to what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now it says under number Roman numeral II that: "... the police in their present formation were not providing security for the citizens." Was that in fact the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not have that impression because the station functioned properly, with the anomalies that I mentioned, but it functioned, and the routine police business was done, as it was supposed to be done, traffic, crime investigation, law enforcement, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that up until the 21st of April, the police force in Vlasenica was multi-ethnic. Did the Muslim police officers at the SJB comply with this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under section reman numeral III, it states that the SJB chief: "Radomir Bjelanovic is hereby authorised to engage the required number of active and reserve forces to secure public law and order and safe-guard the citizens." We've already established that Bjelanovic was a member of the Crisis Staff. What was the reasoning behind this exception for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Mr. Bjelanovic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that he agreed to implement this addition; although, you can see that this decision was taken on the basis of the decision of the Municipal Assembly in Vlasenica, that this was not done in consultation with the higher-up levels at the republic. In other words, it was done at the municipality level, and he probably agreed to implement this decision, in order to change the structure and the composition of the police force, in the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many active and reserve police officers Bjelanovic engaged pursuant to this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure, but the following happened. After this decision, all the police officers of Serb ethnic background were re-employed. They continued working, while the Muslim policemen were laid off or were told to take annual leave. They no longer did their jobs, and they were no longer police officers or shift leaders and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. This would be Exhibit P1060, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, your last comment begs the question as to whether the weapons that had just been collected from the police force were then given back to the Serb policemen, who were then re-employed. Do you know if they were -- if the re-employed Serbian policemen were then given back their weapons that they had just handed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were issued weapons again. Their own, the ones that they had returned, or some other weapons, but it -- I don't know that, but they were issued weapons again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So am I right to understand that this whole operation was designed to -- to rid the SJB in Vlasenica of the Muslim and Croat policemen and retain only the Serbian policemen? Was that the purpose of this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you analyse the situation, yes, it does follow from this decision that the idea was to change the ethnic composition, to disband everyone, and then to take back only those that you wanted to have back on board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move to the day of the takeover. So we're -- now we're on the 21st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us which Serb forces participated in the takeover the Vlasenica town on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on what I know, the members of the JNA took part in those activities. They had some APCs and combat vehicles and a certain number of troops. Members of the Territorial Defence also took part. It was the newly established TO. And the main agent in this job was a paramilitary unit, we might call it that. Later on, I learned that it was called the Serbian Guard from Sekovici. Now whether it was part of a JNA unit that was stationed in Sekovici or not, whether it was some other form of organisation, I don't know. But, at any rate, those were the forces that were involved in that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it's 12.00. It's time for the break. We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before the break, we were talking about the various Serb forces that participated in the takeover on 21 April, and you mentioned that the JNA was participating in the takeover. Could you tell us what corps of the JNA was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called it the Novi Sad Corps. It was a unit provisionally stationed with their command in Sekovici at Ulovnica [phoen] hotel, and they got there after withdrawing from Croatia or wherever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serb guard that you mentioned, could you tell us what kind of uniforms they were wearing and whether they had any arm-bands or any other markings to distinguish themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since it was just the beginning, almost all army troops were still wearing the traditional olive-green-grey uniforms, the so-called SMB colour, and these wore camouflage SMB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb guard have any arm-bands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really remember, but I think that they did have the Serbian Guard insignia on their sleeves. Now, they may have worn a red ribbons on their upper arms, and in that action they also had face paint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these Serb Guards the ones that were at SJB building when you arrived on 21st of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the day of the takeover, or, in fact, the days that immediately followed the takeover, was there any Muslim resistance in Vlasenica town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No armed resistance was recorded. There were no incidents of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long the JNA Novi Sad Corps remained in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Elements of those forces remained there after the 21st, and the entire formation that was stationed there with its headquarters in Sekovici remained there until the 19th of May. And then, on the orders of the then ministry or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it was tasked with leaving the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina but upon its departure, some of the troops and some of the equipment, military equipment, remained there. Whether on a voluntary basis or ... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for us the equipment that they left behind in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, those were infantry weapons, automatic rifles, in military parlance. Rifles, light machine-guns, mortars, a small quantity. There were probably some grenades and a number of small armoured vehicles; armoured personnel carriers, as they were called. And maybe a tank or two, but I can't really say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when were you officially mobilised in the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not mobilised in the RS MUP -- or, rather, I was assigned in the Republika Srpska MUP as early as on -- or around the 23rd or the 24th of April. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you've testified that, after the takeover, the Muslims who worked at SJB Vlasenica were discharged from the police. Approximately how many days after the takeover were all the Muslim, Croat police officers gone from the SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 22nd, or the 23rd, on or around those dates, they were issued decisions that they were on annual leave or administrative leave. They did not return to service because they had been issued those decisions. After the 21st, they no longer served as policemen in the station. They were no longer present there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime around mid-May 1992, did SJB Vlasenica receive an instruction from the RS MUP regarding personnel matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I was taken over, in a manner of speaking, from the former MUP, and in accordance with the mobilisation plan, I was assigned to the Vlasenica station, I had an opportunity later on to find a document, instructions from the Ministry of Interior, describing the manner in which the station is to operate and organise its work in a state of an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who signed that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document that I found was signed by Mico Stanisic, the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could take a look at Exhibit 1D46.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we have before us is an order dated 15 May 1992. Could you tell us whether is this the order that you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what actions did the SJB Vlasenica take, pursuant to this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in light of the fact that Mr. Bjelanovic was chief at the time, transformation and reorganisation was carried out in accordance with the instructions. The existing number of policemen who remained there, who were on active duty, and a certain number of reserve police officers, because some of the active and reserve policemen of Bosniak ethnic background had left, resulting in a decrease in the number of the police, and some of the policemen went to the Milici police station which had been newly established. So there was a small number of active and reserve police officers, and for that reason, a request was made to fill the ranks with the reserve police officers, and a request was put to the ministry to make sure that it is done in order for the police to be able to perform its tasks as required in the newly developed circumstances. And this is why some action was taken in accordance with the order of the minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said that a request was made to fill the ranks with the reserve police officers to the ministry. Did the ministry respond to that request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence, that's what I meant. The Ministry of Defence did respond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I think I understand you. You're saying that the Secretariat of National Defence filled the ranks with the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I believe this has already been admitted into evidence. So let's move on to the next document, which has been marked for identification. It's P1046. I ask this not be broadcast because it does contain the name of the witness. And if we could go to page -- the second page in both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document is entitled: "List of Active Police Workers who Have Worked at this SM," which I believe is police station, "in May 1992 and Who Have Been Paid LD," which is salary, "in Advance of This Month." Sir, do you recognise the name under entry number 1 as yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose signature is at the end of this entry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could scroll over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you mean the signature up there, under number 1, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page. Just over to the right a little bit. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see a signature in the right-hand corner. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the rest of the names on this page are a little bit illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So why don't we move to the next page, page 3. I think it's a clearer copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see here 27 names of active police workers on this list. What are their ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to this list, who was police commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commander, komandir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, who was police commander at SJB Vlasenica in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the commander? The Serbian word would be komandir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radenko Stanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Radenko Stanic's relation to the president of the Crisis Staff, Milenko Stanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was chief of the crime service at the SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milenko Sargic. But I can't really say who was issued the appropriate decision, at what time. And I believe that those -- since those workers had already been employed in the Vlasenica public security station at the time, and then they continued working in accordance with the previously issued decisions as the minister issued the decision adopting the rules on the internal organisation and final decisions in accordance with the Law on the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska or the Republic of BiH only at a later stage. But the acting chief of crime service was Milenko Sargic, and Radenko Stanic was the commander of the police station. However, I'm not sure when they actually received the decisions to that effect. Probably it was at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thank you for that clarification. Who did Stanic and Sargic report to within the SJB Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in this period, while Radomir Bjelanovic was the chief, at one point he was appointed the coordinator for the Birac region. That would be the -- he was assistant to the centre chief, Cvijetic, and he would go there from time to time, and he would also visit the Milici station. If there were any problems, they were reported to Mr. Bjelanovic, and then, later on, he probably reported to the centre chief, Cvijetic, and then up the chain of command, and great deal of emphasis was placed on that, Cvijetic would report to the minister, if he saw fit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't see Radomir Bjelanovic listed here on this list. In fact we have you listed as chief of the police on this list. Where was Bjelanovic? Where did he go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time he spent most of his time in the Milici police station because it was in the process of being set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did he become chief of police at SJB Milici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that, at the period when I was issued my decision or maybe earlier, it was all regulated. When the framework rules were adopted, the minister issued the appropriate decision. In my case it was on the 8th of August, and I'm sure that the same thing happened for Mr. Bjelanovic, because, at that point in time, the police stations started functioning independently, separately, each had its own separate internal structure and organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned that you were officially appointed chief of SJB Vlasenica on 8 August 1992. On this document, for May 1992, you -- you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It designates you as chief of the station. You were given a salary of chief and you signed it chief. Who gave you the right or the authorisation to perform that role prior to August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the new rules were adopted, the coordination and the functioning of the police went in accordance with the procedure that was in place. Mr. Bjelanovic authorised me, since he had already been appointed coordinator, to adopt certain acts that were not of vital importance and to do some tasks of that nature. And later on, in conversation with Mr. Cvijetic, the chief, the centre chief, who came to the station, he said that he would put my name forward with the minister, that he would recommend that a decision be issued to me appointing me the chief of the public security station in Vlasenica. So at that time it was my task to act as a coordinator, or whatever, but so -- in agreement with Mr. Bjelanovic and the centre chief, I was to do that job until such time when I was issued the final decision. An example that could not affect strategy or the overall success of the defence effort in that area was, for instance, this signing a document such as this one, or the payroll.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand your testimony correctly, Bjelanovic authorised you to submit payrolls and perform other functions that would normally be responsibilities of the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I could not make decisions without consulting him and further up the chain of command. I could only do some co-ordinating in order for the police station to be set up properly and to start functioning properly as a professional police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you had a take a decision that went beyond that, you would have to get the authorisation of Bjelanovic. Would you also have to have the authorisation of the CSB chief, Zoran Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the MUP, there is the subordination system, and logic dictates that the chain of command had to be obeyed. Bjelanovic was my immediate superior because he was the chief of the police station, but he was also the co-ordinator for the Birac region, and then I would explain my reason -- reasons to him, and then he would address the centre chief, and then further on, the minister, lest I should, God forbid, address the centre chief or even the minister myself, because that would mean skipping some of the levels in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question about this list. Under number 20 is there is a Sinisa Miljanic. Could you tell me was that individual an active police officer before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. But I know that later on he attended some kind of training, which means that he was a reserve police officer. He was a younger man. And all those lads, once the rules were adopted, and once MUP became better organised, they were all sent for police training. And I, in fact, believe that he is to this day a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, you called this document to the screen with, if I'm not wrong, an exhibit number, a P number, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What was the P number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, sorry about that. It is P1046. It was only marked for identification. It was 65 ter 2814. The reason it probably on your list didn't show up is because it was marked earlier this week for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now in addition to the active police workers at SJB Vlasenica --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- Exhibit P1046 will be now admitted under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the active police workers at SJB Vlasenica, what other police units existed within the framework of SJB Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there's the active force and the reserve force. And later on, there was will also the intervention platoon, which was called the special police unit, or the special purpose unit. And we will see later on how this unit came into being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning first to the reserve police force. Could you tell us approximately how large the reserve police force was from May through, let's say, September 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number varied occasionally, as the circumstances in the region changed. At the moment, for instance, when the Army of Republika Srpska was established a smaller number was required, but there was 70 to 80 reserve policemen at that time, on the average.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of this reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's clear by now after that overhaul on the 21st of April, they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you briefly describe generally what were the responsibilities of the reserve police after -- well, let's say, after the takeover on 21 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tasks of the reserve policemen, since they had some prior police training from the past because they had gone through training, were similar to the tasks of the active force.
